title: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
description_short: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
description_medium: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent Federal Election Commission chair Ellen Weintraub a letter saying she was removed immediately. Weintraub disputed the president’s authority to fire her, and a former Republican FEC chair also called the move unlawful. The timing drew scrutiny because the commission was preparing to consider complaints involving Trump’s campaign and political spending.
description_long: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent a letter to Federal Election Commission Chair Ellen Weintraub — a Democratic commissioner who had been an outspoken critic of Trump's campaign finance violations — stating You are hereby removed as a Member of the Federal Election Commission, effective immediately. Weintraub publicly rejected the removal as illegal, noting that no president had ever fired an FEC commissioner and that the Federal Election Campaign Act contained no firing authority for the president. Republican former FEC Chair Trevor Potter called the action contrary to law, noting that Trump was free to nominate a replacement but could not simply fire a sitting commissioner. The timing was significant: the FEC was preparing to consider complaints against Trump's 2024 campaign and against Elon Musk's $277 million in political spending. Weintraub lost her email, computer, and cellphone access by February 7. The move was part of a broader pattern of firing independent agency members and preceded the eventual July 2026 Supreme Court ruling that gave presidents expanded power to fire independent agency members.

title: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process
description_short: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process
description_medium: In March 2025, the administration sent 137 Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador’s CECOT prison under the Alien Enemies Act without hearings or a chance to challenge removal. A federal judge had ordered flights blocked, but aircraft continued. Courts later found the men were denied due process, and the Supreme Court agreed they were entitled to notice and an opportunity to contest deportation.
description_long: On March 15–16, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act — not used since World War II — to deport 137 Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador's CECOT prison with no notice, no hearings, and no opportunity to challenge removal. Federal Judge James Boasberg had issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, and evidence emerged that planes carrying detainees had been ordered to continue to El Salvador even after the TRO was issued. In June 2025, Boasberg ruled in a sweeping opinion that the men had been plainly deprived of due process rights, comparing their situation to a Kafka novel: Perhaps the President lawfully invoked the Alien Enemies Act. Perhaps, moreover, Defendants are correct that Plaintiffs are gang members. But there is simply no way to know for sure, as the CECOT Plaintiffs never had any opportunity to challenge the Government's say-so. The Supreme Court unanimously agreed the men were entitled to notice and the opportunity to challenge removal before deportation. The administration had given some detainees as little as 24 hours notice.

title: Trump Tower Russia Meeting: Don Jr. Takes a Meeting to Get Dirt on Clinton
description_short: Trump Tower Russia Meeting: Don Jr. Takes a Meeting to Get Dirt on Clinton
description_medium: On June 9, 2016, Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, and campaign chair Paul Manafort met a Russian lawyer at Trump Tower after being offered information described as part of Russia’s support for Donald Trump. Trump Jr. replied, “If it’s what you say I love it.” Senate investigators later found no reliable evidence that useful information was transmitted or that Trump knew of the meeting in advance.
description_long: On June 9, 2016, Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, and then-campaign chairman Paul Manafort met at Trump Tower in New York with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya, after British music publicist Rob Goldstone emailed Trump Jr. that the meeting would provide official documents and information that would incriminate Hillary as part of Russia and its government's support for Mr. Trump. Trump Jr. responded by email: If it's what you say I love it especially later in the summer. The meeting was attended by at least eight people, including a former Soviet intelligence officer. Trump Jr. initially told the Senate Judiciary Committee he could not recall discussing it with his father. The meeting — kept secret until the New York Times reported it in July 2017, prompting Trump Jr. to release his emails — represented the most direct documented evidence of the Trump campaign's willingness to accept foreign interference in a U.S. election. The Senate Intelligence Committee later concluded in 2020 that Manafort's sharing of internal polling data with a Russian associate with GRU ties constituted a grave counterintelligence threat.

title: North Korea Rejects Denuclearization, Demands US Accept Nuclear Reality
description_short: North Korea Rejects Denuclearization, Demands US Accept Nuclear Reality
description_medium: North Korean official Kim Yo Jong said in July 2025 that future talks would not end the country’s nuclear weapons program, despite President Trump’s interest in another summit with Kim Jong Un. Pyongyang urged Washington to accept its nuclear status. The statement underscored the gap between Trump’s denuclearization goal and North Korea’s public position, while relations between Pyongyang and Moscow were also deepening.
description_long: On July 28–29, 2025, North Korea's Kim Yo Jong — believed to speak for her brother, Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un — publicly dismissed US hopes for denuclearization talks, stating that no future dialogue would end North Korea's nuclear weapons program. Responding to Trump's repeated overtures for a summit, Kim Yo Jong conceded that the personal relationship between Kim and Trump is not bad, but warned that any attempt to use personal diplomacy to end the nuclear program would only be subject of mockery. She demanded the US accept the changed reality. North Korea had entered 2025 with Kim ordering increased production of weapons-grade nuclear material in January; analysts estimated Pyongyang had enough material for up to 90 warheads. Trump expressed desire to meet Kim this year while simultaneously maintaining a stated goal of complete denuclearization — a position Kim had explicitly rejected as impossible. Meanwhile, North Korea had deepened its military and diplomatic ties with Russia, including deploying troops to support Russian forces in Ukraine, giving Pyongyang new geopolitical leverage the Trump administration was unable to effectively counter.

title: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
description_short: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
description_medium: After President Trump signed an order targeting the U.S. Agency for Global Media on March 14, 2025, all 1,300 Voice of America employees were placed on leave the next morning and barred from the newsroom. VOA director Michael Abramowitz said the broadcaster was being silenced for the first time in 83 years. The shutdown threatened a service that reached audiences in 47 languages.
description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order gutting the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), Voice of America's parent. By the morning of March 15, all 1,300 VOA employees had been placed on paid administrative leave, barred from the building and their equipment. DOGE operative Gavin Kliger — a former Twitter engineer — had been spotted inside VOA headquarters weeks earlier. VOA director Michael Abramowitz stated: For the first time in 83 years, the storied Voice of America is being silenced. Kari Lake, Trump's loyalist USAGM adviser, signed termination notices and canceled the agency's 15-year lease. VOA had operated continuously since 1942, originally to counter Nazi propaganda, and reached an estimated 247 million people weekly in 47 languages. Russian state media celebrated the shutdown; China's state press called VOA a dirty rag. The National Press Club said the action undermines America's long-standing commitment to a free press. Courts had blocked similar USAGM dismantlement attempts during Trump's first term. The shutdown left audiences across authoritarian states without access to independent, U.S.-funded journalism precisely when such coverage mattered most.

title: FBI Director Kash Patel Promotes Unverified CCP 2020 Election Conspiracy Theory
description_short: FBI Director Kash Patel Promotes Unverified CCP 2020 Election Conspiracy Theory
description_medium: On June 17, 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel publicized an unverified tip alleging Chinese involvement in a 2020 fake-ID voting scheme. The cited evidence involved counterfeit IDs that Customs and Border Protection attributed to underage students seeking alcohol. Election experts said the tip was unsubstantiated, and former FBI officials warned against presenting raw allegations as established intelligence.
description_long: On June 17, 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel published a post claiming the FBI had located alarming documents alleging Chinese Communist Party interference in the 2020 election. Patel said he had immediately declassified the material and shared it with Sen. Chuck Grassley. The documents centered on an unverified 2020 tip from an anonymous confidential informant claiming China mass-produced fake driver's licenses for a mail-in ballot scheme. NBC News and election law experts noted the tip was never substantiated: the only evidence Patel cited was CBP seizures of fake IDs from China, which CBP itself attributed to underage college students seeking to purchase alcohol. Election law expert Rick Hasen said Patel's post might feed the MAGA base but amounted to promoting an uncorroborated story of unknown origin with no evidence that anything actually happened. Two former senior FBI officials noted the bureau receives hundreds of tips daily, many unverified, and one warned that publicizing this information played into the hands of our foreign enemies. No evidence of widespread 2020 voter fraud has been found by any investigation, including those conducted by Trump-appointed officials.

title: Trump: Starmer’s slow start in the war against Iran could leave UK playing catch-up
description_short: Trump: Starmer’s slow start in the war against Iran could leave UK playing catch-up
description_medium: A March 2026 Guardian report examined Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s initial reluctance to support U.S. action against Iran and the pressure it could create for Britain. The article said U.S. carrier deployments signaled preparations for a possible conflict while British forces were more limited. It framed the issue as a risk to the UK’s ability to protect citizens in the Gulf and reassure allies.
description_long: Starmer’s slow start in the war against Iran could leave UK playing catch-up. Prime minister’s initial refusal to help US could constrain Britain’s ability to protect its nationals in the Gulf and reassure allies Middle East crisis – live updates Britain knew that the US was considering attacking Iran from the moment Donald Trump told protesters that “help is coming” in the middle of January. It was obvious to the world that the White House was serious when the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group was sent to the Arabian Sea in late January. But as Trump gradually built up his “massive armada”, reinforcing it with a second carrier strike group in mid-February, UK deployments were constrained and limited even though there was a recognition that it was likely allies and bases with British soldiers would be attacked in an Iranian retaliation. Continue reading... This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.

title: Clean Power Plan 2.0 Gutted — EPA Proposes Eliminating All GHG Standards for Power Plants
description_short: Clean Power Plan 2.0 Gutted — EPA Proposes Eliminating All GHG Standards for Power Plants
description_medium: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin proposed repealing greenhouse-gas standards for power plants and 2024 amendments to mercury limits for coal plants. Zeldin said the changes would save utilities $120 million annually; environmental groups warned of higher toxic pollution and health risks. The proposal would roll back rules under the Clean Air Act, pending public review and final agency action.
description_long: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, flanked by Republican lawmakers at EPA headquarters, proposed repealing all greenhouse gas emissions standards for the U.S. power sector under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act — effectively eliminating both the 2015 Obama-era standards for new fossil fuel plants and Biden's 2024 Clean Power Plan 2.0 emission guidelines for existing coal, oil, and gas plants. The proposal also moved to repeal 2024 amendments to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards that had been requiring coal plants to reduce brain-damaging mercury emissions. Zeldin claimed the rollbacks would save $120 million per year for electric utilities. Environmental groups countered that the repeals would increase cancer-causing and neurotoxic air pollution, lock in decades of carbon emissions, and kill thousands of Americans prematurely each year from worsened air quality. EPA had telegraphed the move on March 12, 2025, when Zeldin announced it as part of what he called the most consequential day of deregulation in U.S. history. A public hearing on the GHG repeal was held July 8, 2025, with EPA planning to finalize the rule by spring 2026.

title: DHS Secretary Mullin Threatens State Election Officials With Arrest Weeks Before 2026 Midterms
description_short: DHS Secretary Mullin Threatens State Election Officials With Arrest Weeks Before 2026 Midterms
description_medium: In July 2026, the Department of Homeland Security threatened state election officials with funding losses or investigations if they did not adopt federal voter-roll measures. A July 17 statement by Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned officials in four states of fines or criminal charges. The demands included checks against a federal citizenship database that experts had criticized as error-prone, shortly before the 2026 midterms.
description_long: On July 8, 2026, the Trump administration sent letters to state election officials warning that officials could face arrest if they failed to purge noncitizens from voter rolls using a federal DHS database that experts had criticized as error-prone. The administration simultaneously threatened to withhold tens of millions of dollars in Homeland Security grant funding from states that refused to adopt sweeping election changes — including phasing out electronic voting machines and running all voter rolls through DHS's citizenship verification system. On July 17, 2026, one day after Trump's primetime televised speech on election fraud, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin escalated from the White House podium, warning state officials they could lose funding or face investigations for non-compliance just months before November midterms. UCLA law professor Rick Hasen said Trump was trying to use whatever levers of power and persuasive power he might have to interfere with how states and localities are going to conduct the 2026 election. Federal courts had already blocked most of the administration's voting restrictions, but the threats themselves were designed to create chaos and compliance through fear, independent of legal outcome.

title: Riyadh Sellout: Trump Negotiates Ukraine's Fate with Russia, Excluding Europe and Kyiv
description_short: Riyadh Sellout: Trump Negotiates Ukraine's Fate with Russia, Excluding Europe and Kyiv
description_medium: President Trump announced direct U.S.-Russia talks over Ukraine after calling Vladimir Putin on February 12, 2025. At a February 18 meeting in Riyadh, U.S. and Russian officials discussed ending the war without Ukrainian or European representatives at the table. The exclusion drew criticism from European leaders and raised concerns that decisions affecting Ukraine’s territory and security were being negotiated without Ukraine.
description_long: On February 12, 2025, Trump called Vladimir Putin and announced the start of direct U.S.-Russia negotiations to end the Ukraine war — without notifying NATO allies or Ukraine's government in advance. On February 18, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, national security adviser Mike Waltz, and special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian counterparts in Riyadh for over four hours, explicitly excluding Ukrainian and European officials from the table. Russia used the talks to harden demands, insisting NATO cancel its 2008 promise to eventually admit Ukraine, and demanding territorial concessions. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas declared any deal behind our backs will not work, while Foreign Policy analysts described the episode as the most comprehensive remaking of Europe's security landscape since NATO expansion in the 1990s. Trump had already ruled out NATO membership for Ukraine, demanded Ukraine surrender occupied territory, and proposed transferring vast portions of Ukrainian natural resources to the United States. European leaders warned that Trump appeared to believe giving Putin much of what he wants in Europe was the best path forward, effectively rewarding illegal aggression and demolishing 80 years of post-war security architecture.

title: DOGE Copied All 548 Million SSNs to Unsecured Cloud Without Oversight
description_short: DOGE Copied All 548 Million SSNs to Unsecured Cloud Without Oversight
description_medium: A Social Security Administration whistleblower alleged that DOGE-affiliated staff copied the NUMIDENT database, containing 548 million Social Security numbers and identifying details, to an Amazon cloud environment without verified security oversight. The transfer followed a Supreme Court ruling allowing access. A security officer had warned of identity-theft risks, while the agency disputed parts of the characterization but confirmed the environment existed.
description_long: In August 2025, Social Security Administration Chief Data Officer Charles Borges filed a whistleblower complaint with Congress alleging that DOGE officials employed as SSA staff had copied the entire NUMIDENT database — containing 548 million Social Security numbers along with names, addresses, dates of birth, parents' names, and other identifying information for every living and dead American who ever had an SSN — to a custom Amazon Web Services cloud environment that lacked any verified security oversight. The transfer occurred after the Supreme Court's June 6, 2025 ruling lifted a lower-court injunction blocking DOGE's SSA access. The acting chief information security officer had formally flagged the request as high risk and warned it could make Americans vulnerable to identity theft, but DOGE-affiliated CIO Aram Moghaddassi and Michael Russo approved the transfer anyway, arguing the business need is higher than the security risk. No independent security monitoring was in place; no one outside the DOGE group had insight into the code being executed against live SSA production data. Borges received no response to his security concerns from DOGE-affiliated staff. The SSA's spokesperson disputed the characterization but confirmed the environment existed.

title: Trump Pressures Texas Redistricting to Flip 5 Democratic House Seats, Igniting National Map-Drawing Arms Race
description_short: Trump Pressures Texas Redistricting to Flip 5 Democratic House Seats, Igniting National Map-Drawing Arms Race
description_medium: In July 2025, Texas Republicans pursued a mid-decade congressional map at President Trump’s urging, aiming to gain five House seats for the GOP before the 2026 elections. Trump also pressed other Republican-led states, and Indiana’s lieutenant governor said officials threatened federal funding over redistricting. Democratic governors discussed counter-maps, setting off a national fight over partisan district lines and federal pressure on state election policy.
description_long: In July 2025, at Trump's direct urging, Texas Republicans undertook an extraordinary mid-decade redraw of the state's congressional districts, targeting five Democratic-held U.S. House seats with the explicit goal of protecting the GOP's fragile House majority ahead of the 2026 midterms — a move upending decades of precedent against mid-cycle partisan redistricting. Trump applied direct pressure to multiple other Republican-controlled legislatures; in Indiana, Lieutenant Governor Micah Beckwith confirmed that unnamed Trump administration officials threatened the state's federal funding if it refused to redistrict. The gambit ignited a national redistricting arms race, with Democratic governors — led by California's Gavin Newsom — threatening retaliatory redraws in blue states. Meanwhile, Trump's administration and the Republican-controlled Congress continued to block Puerto Rico statehood and Washington DC statehood, both of which would add likely Democratic senators and representatives; Puerto Rico's statehood referendum had been approved by voters in November 2024 but the 119th Congress refused to act. The Votebeat analysis found that Trump had become the most interventionist president in the history of state election administration, directly threatening officials by name and promising to support primary challengers against Republicans who resisted his redistricting demands.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Pressures Texas Redistricting to Flip 5 Democratic House Seats, Igniting National Map-Drawing Arms Race
preserved_fields.description_long: In July 2025, at Trump's direct urging, Texas Republicans undertook an extraordinary mid-decade redraw of the state's congressional districts, targeting five Democratic-held U.S. House seats with the explicit goal of protecting the GOP's fragile House majority ahead of the 2026 midterms — a move upending decades of precedent against mid-cycle partisan redistricting. Trump applied direct pressure to multiple other Republican-controlled legislatures; in Indiana, Lieutenant Governor Micah Beckwith confirmed that unnamed Trump administration officials threatened the state's federal funding if it refused to redistrict. The gambit ignited a national redistricting arms race, with Democratic governors — led by California's Gavin Newsom — threatening retaliatory redraws in blue states. Meanwhile, Trump's administration and the Republican-controlled Congress continued to block Puerto Rico statehood and Washington DC statehood, both of which would add likely Democratic senators and representatives; Puerto Rico's statehood referendum had been approved by voters in November 2024 but the 119th Congress refused to act. The Votebeat analysis found that Trump had become the most interventionist president in the history of state election administration, directly threatening officials by name and promising to support primary challengers against Republicans who resisted his redistricting demands.

title: White House Systematically Deploys AI Deepfakes as Official Government Communications
description_short: White House Systematically Deploys AI Deepfakes as Official Government Communications
description_medium: A PolitiFact review counted dozens of AI-generated posts from Trump’s Truth Social and the White House’s X account during 2025, including fabricated depictions of political opponents. Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt defended the content as memes, while Trump also suggested an actual video might be AI. The pattern blurred the line between official communication, satire, and synthetic media presented to the public.
description_long: Beginning in early 2025, the Trump White House formally adopted AI-generated deepfakes and synthetic media as standard government communications tools. PolitiFact's October 2025 analysis documented 36 AI posts from Trump's Truth Social since inauguration, with the White House X account and DHS also regularly publishing AI-fabricated imagery. Content included: an AI fake of Nancy Pelosi falsely claiming to admit insider trading crimes (September 8, 2025); a deepfake of Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer in sombreros with fake audio (September 29, 2025, reshared 19,400 times); Trump as pope after Francis's death; a cartoon of Trump firing Fed Chair Jerome Powell; and a video of Trump dumping feces on protesters. Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt defended the practice, stating Trump's sharing of AI content was quite refreshing. When asked about an actual White House maintenance video, Trump falsely attributed it to AI, then mused if something happens really bad, maybe I'll have to just blame AI. The White House posted on X on July 11, 2025: Nowhere in the Constitution does it say we can't post banger memes. The memes will continue. House Speaker Mike Johnson defended the practice as satire.

title: Trump Sues Wall Street Journal for $10B, Bans Reporter from Scotland Trip
description_short: Trump Sues Wall Street Journal for $10B, Bans Reporter from Scotland Trip
description_medium: On July 18, 2025, Trump sued the Wall Street Journal and its owners and reporters for $10 billion over a story about a birthday note attributed to him. Days later, the White House excluded a Journal reporter from Trump’s Scotland trip press pool. The lawsuit and access restriction followed the report, prompting press groups to object to punitive treatment of a news organization.
description_long: On July 18, 2025, Trump filed a $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, its parent company News Corp, publisher Almar Latour, two reporters, and owner Rupert Murdoch over a July 17 article reporting that a 2003 birthday album gifted to Jeffrey Epstein included a note bearing Trump's name with a sexually suggestive drawing. Trump denied the letter's authenticity. The following Monday, July 21, the White House used its seized control of press pool assignments to ban WSJ reporter Tarini Parti from covering Trump's four-day trip to his golf courses in Turnberry and Aberdeen, Scotland. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt cited fake and defamatory conduct. The WHCA urged the White House to restore WSJ's position. The Wall Street Journal had been a regular pool participant until the Epstein story broke. The lawsuit named Rupert Murdoch — nominally a Trump ally — illustrating that even outlets within conservative media ecosystems were not immune to retaliation. Press groups noted the chilling paradox: the president who had promised to end censorship was suing a major newspaper over a story about a convicted sex trafficker while simultaneously using presidential access control as a punitive weapon.

title: US Citizens Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez and Jose Hermosillo Detained by ICE Despite Documentation
description_short: US Citizens Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez and Jose Hermosillo Detained by ICE Despite Documentation
description_medium: Two U.S. citizens, Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez and Jose Hermosillo, were detained by immigration authorities in 2025 despite citizenship documents or later proof. Lopez-Gomez was held more than 30 hours after presenting identification, and a judge found no probable cause for the detainer. Hermosillo was held for 10 days before his family secured his release. The cases contradicted an official claim that no citizens had been arrested.
description_long: A documented pattern of ICE detaining American citizens swept through 2025. Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, 20, born in Georgia, was arrested on April 16 during a traffic stop in Florida under a state law that a federal judge had already suspended on April 4. He presented his Social Security card and Georgia REAL ID to police but was held for more than 30 hours. ICE placed a detainer on the jail even after a judge found no probable cause. DHS falsely claimed Lopez-Gomez had identified himself as undocumented. Jose Hermosillo, 19, of Albuquerque, was arrested by Border Patrol in Tucson on April 9 while visiting with his girlfriend — 70 miles from the Mexican border — and held for 10 days before his family secured his release by providing proof of citizenship. DHS alleged Hermosillo told an agent he was born in Mexico; Hermosillo denied it, and attorneys noted he has a learning disability. In May 2026, a top ICE official stated at a border security conference: Since the start of this administration, we have not had any arrests of U.S. citizens... That's happened zero times — a claim directly contradicted by available evidence.

title: Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50%, Gutting Downstream Industries
description_short: Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50%, Gutting Downstream Industries
description_medium: On June 4, 2025, President Trump raised steel and aluminum import tariffs from 25% to 50%, saying the duties would protect domestic producers. The higher costs affected manufacturers and other industries that use metals, with companies reporting added expenses and price increases. The supplied account links the tariffs to job losses, layoffs, and delayed investment downstream, alongside gains for some domestic producers.
description_long: On June 4, 2025, Trump doubled U.S. tariffs on all steel and aluminum imports from 25% to 50% — among the highest metal duties in American history — just months after reinstating the original 25% rates in February. The stated goal was protecting domestic steel and aluminum producers, but economic analysis was clear about the consequences for downstream industries. A study found Trump's first-term steel tariffs created roughly 1,000 jobs in the steel sector while destroying 75,000 jobs in steel-using industries like manufacturing, construction, and auto parts. The 50% tariff added an estimated $2,000+ in production costs per vehicle. The aluminum tariff alone added $3,000 to the cost of an F-150 truck. John Deere cited $300 million in tariff-related costs in August 2025 and announced layoffs at Illinois and Iowa plants. Companies like Jordan Manufacturing in Belding, Michigan, saw steel prices rise 5%–10% and were forced to raise customer prices 8%–14%. The Tax Foundation's Erica York said: It's just very foolish to double down on this type of tariff in particular. Canada's steel and aluminum industry faced mass layoffs and investment deferrals. U.S. construction contracted 3.6% in long-run projections from the Yale Budget Lab.

title: Green Card Holders Detained for Decades-Old Minor Crimes; LPRs Fear Leaving US
description_short: Green Card Holders Detained for Decades-Old Minor Crimes; LPRs Fear Leaving US
description_medium: Lawful permanent residents faced increased scrutiny and detention when returning to the United States, including for old or minor records. Lewelyn Dixon, a green-card holder, was held for nearly three months after disclosing a decades-old conviction; Columbia student Yunseo Chung faced an effort to revoke her status over protest activity. A judge barred Chung’s detention while she challenged the action, and attorneys reported clients feared traveling abroad.
description_long: Under Trump's second term, Customs and Border Protection and ICE sharply escalated enforcement against lawful permanent residents upon reentry, targeting people with decades-old criminal records that had previously been overlooked. Lewelyn Dixon, a 64-year-old Filipina legal permanent resident, was arrested at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and held for nearly three months after she disclosed a past workplace theft conviction from years prior, despite having lived blamelessly in her American community since. Her attorney noted he had handled three similar cases since February 2025 alone — unprecedented in his 12-year career. The pattern extended to Green Card holders with minor resolved records facing surprise detention when attempting to re-enter from international travel. Yunseo Chung, a 21-year-old Korean American Columbia University student who had lived in the U.S. since age seven as a lawful permanent resident, had her LPR status revocation initiated by DHS over pro-Palestinian protest participation. A federal judge ruled on March 25, 2025 that Chung could not be detained while fighting the revocation. Immigration attorneys reported a flood of clients asking whether they could safely leave the country at all — a chilling effect on the freedom of movement of 13 million legal permanent residents.

title: Tariffs Weaponized for Corporate Allies: Chevron, Starlink in Trade Deals
description_short: Tariffs Weaponized for Corporate Allies: Chevron, Starlink in Trade Deals
description_medium: Internal trade-negotiation documents reported by the Washington Post included requests that foreign governments provide advantages to U.S. companies such as Chevron and Elon Musk’s Starlink. The objectives also linked tariff pressure to energy, defense, and security demands. The disclosures raised concerns that trade policy was being used to advance particular corporate interests alongside government goals, rather than solely to negotiate general market access.
description_long: Internal documents obtained by The Washington Post in August 2025 revealed that Trump's trade team had weaponized tariff negotiations to secure business advantages for politically connected corporations. In eight-page supplemental negotiating objectives for trade talks with India, U.S. officials demanded India halt oil purchases from Russia — or face 50% tariffs — while separately pushing India, Taiwan, and Indonesia to purchase more American military equipment. Most remarkably, the documents showed Chevron's business interests were embedded directly in trade negotiating objectives with multiple foreign governments, asking them to avoid regulations that could harm Chevron's operations. Elon Musk's Starlink was flagged for favorable telecommunications licensing treatment abroad, including waiving physical-presence requirements in some markets. Israel and Australia were pressed to remove Chinese control from key ports. African and South American nations were pushed to limit Chinese telecom and military ties. Cambodia was told tariff relief was contingent on U.S. Navy port access. Officials described the scope as shocking. The blending of personal corporate interests, political alliances, and ostensibly public trade policy represented what critics called a textbook crony capitalist system in which tariff rates were effectively for sale to those who provided the right political or business concessions.

title: Trump Freezes $175M to UPenn Over Lia Thomas, Forces Record Erasure
description_short: Trump Freezes $175M to UPenn Over Lia Thomas, Forces Record Erasure
description_medium: The Trump administration froze about $175 million in Penn funding in March 2025 over the university’s transgender-athlete policies, then released the money after a July agreement. Penn agreed to restrict future participation and remove Lia Thomas’s NCAA championship records. The use of federal grants to obtain changes to athletic policy and historical records drew protests and raised concerns about university autonomy.
description_long: On March 19, 2025, the Trump administration announced it was suspending approximately $175 million in federal funding to the University of Pennsylvania — money drawn from the Department of Defense and the Department of Health and Human Services — over the school's past support of transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, who had last competed for Penn in 2022, three years earlier. Thomas had won the 2022 NCAA championship in the women's 500-yard freestyle, making her the first transgender woman to win an NCAA swimming championship. A White House official cited Thomas's access to the locker room as part of the justification. After months of standoff, on July 1, 2025, the Trump administration released the frozen funds after Penn reached an agreement with the federal government that included blocking transgender athletes from female sports teams going forward and — in a historically unprecedented act — erasing the NCAA championship records set by Thomas. The administration used financial coercion to compel a private university to retroactively revise the historical athletic record to conform to its ideological preferences. Penn students and faculty held protests against the capitulation. The episode set a chilling precedent for academic and institutional autonomy under federal funding pressure.

title: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased
description_short: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased
description_medium: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed a law repealing EPA’s Waste Emissions Charge, which had imposed a fee on excess methane emissions from oil and gas operations. The repeal eliminated a federal financial incentive intended to reduce methane leaks, including at roughly 900,000 wells. The EPA later removed the rule, while oil and gas trade groups welcomed its repeal.
description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed H.J.Res. 35 — a Congressional Review Act joint resolution — into law as Public Law 119-2, nullifying EPA's Waste Emissions Charge rule that had imposed a $900-per-ton fee on oil and gas producers releasing excess methane, a fee that would have escalated to $1,500 per ton by 2026. The WEC had been a centerpiece of the Inflation Reduction Act's climate provisions, representing the first-ever federal price on methane pollution, which traps 80 times more heat per molecule than CO2 over a 20-year period. The House had passed the resolution February 26, 2025, and the Senate followed party-line 52-47 on February 27, with the repeal introduced by Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX). On May 12, 2025, EPA formally removed the WEC regulations from the Code of Federal Regulations. Scientists estimated the methane fee, had it remained in force, would have incentivized dramatic reductions in leaks from the roughly 900,000 U.S. oil and gas wells — methane being responsible for roughly 30% of current global warming. The repeal was celebrated by major oil and gas trade groups and came the same week the administration was proposing separate rollbacks on power plant emissions and vehicle standards.
